arXiv:2503.04077v1 [math.SG] 6 Mar 2025

Periodic Inscription of Isosceles Trapezoids

Ali Naseri Sadr

Abstract We prove that a pair of continuous disjoint periodic curves in C inscribes an isosceles trapezoid with any similarity type. The case of smooth curves can be identified with a Lagrangian intersection problem for a pair of Lagrangian cylinders in R × S' × C, and the continuous case follows from the smooth one by a standard convergence argument.

1 Introduction

Let Y1, 1½: R → C be two continuous embeddings of the real line into C that satisfy the periodicity condition

Vi(t + 1) = Vi(t) + V-1

for every t and i = 1,2. Furthermore, assume the images of Yi and 1½ are disjoint. Tao conjectured in [10] that there exist four points in y1(R) (R)U 1½(R) which are vertices of a square; this is a variation of the Toeplitz square peg problem for periodic curves, and Hugelmeyer proved it in 5]. For any given isosceles trapezoid Q, we show there are four points in yI (R)U 12(R) that are vertices of a quadrilateral similar to Q. The approach of [5] does not directly generalize even to the case of rectangles. By contrast, in this article, we use a different approach to prove not only that every pair of periodic curves inscribes every similarity type of rectangles, but also every similarity type of isosceles trapezoids.

Definition 1.1. Assume Q is an isosceles trapezoid. We say that the pair (V1, 72) admits a balanced inscription of Q if there exist p1, p2 E V1(R) and p3,P4 E Y2(R) such that the quadrilateral formed by p1, pz, p3, P4 is similar to Q, the line segments PIPz and P3P4 are parallel, and [DIPz| ≤ [P3P4|.

Note that our definition depends on the order of the pair (71, 7½) unless Q is a rectangle.

Theorem 1.2. Suppose Y1 and 1½ are two continuous disjoint periodic embeddings of the real line into the plane, and suppose Q is an isosceles trapezoid. Then (Y1, Y2) admits a balanced inscription of Q. Furthermore, there is a generic subset of smooth disjoint periodic pairs such that each pair in this set admits at least two balanced inscriptions of Q that are not related under translation by v

Corollary 1.3. Let 0 € (0, F]; then every pair of continuous disjoint periodic curves in the plane inscribes a rectangle with angle 0 between its two diagonals.

We conjecture that Theorem 1.2 is optimal, in the following sense.

Conjecture 1.4. Let Q be a quadrilateral that admits an inscription in any pair of disjoint periodic curves in C. Then Q is an isosceles trapezoid.
